facts.text: Yorkville got its name from its position north of York Hill, an early term for the elevated land east of what is now Park Avenue.
By the late 19th century, Yorkville had become the heart of Kleindeutschland—New York’s Little Germany—after many German immigrants relocated uptown from the East Village.
Tenement housing predominated east of Third Avenue while the 1837 New York & Harlem Railroad and 1878 Third Avenue Elevated Line spurred rapid urbanization.
Along East 86th Street, bakeries, beer halls, and delicatessens flourished, transforming the thoroughfare into the “German Broadway.”.
Yorkville boasts architecturally distinctive buildings, many of which the Friends of the Upper East Side has sought landmark status for, highlighting its European immigrant heritage.
Sleek stations at 86th and 96th Streets spurred renewed investment, blending new glass towers with preserved brownstones.
